You express emotions (joy, fear, regret, surprise, impatience) with “que” + subjunctive or with “de” + infinitive, depending on whether the subject changes.
to look forward to, can’t wait to
I can’t wait for the concert to start.
I’m afraid of making a mistake.
It’s a pity Mrs Roux can’t come.
We are proud that you played here.
To express emotions with “que” + subjunctive when the subject changes: je suis content que tu sois là.
To use “de” + infinitive when the subject is the same: je suis content d’être là.
To use the past infinitive for an emotion about a past fact: je suis fier d’avoir joué.
To express fear: avoir peur que (+ expletive ne), craindre que.
To express impatience, regret and surprise: avoir hâte, regretter, s’étonner, c’est dommage.
Sunday, 6 April 2030, 3:40 p.m., at the Philharmonie de Paris. The concert starts in twenty minutes. In the orchestra’s dressing room, the children are dressed in black. Inès can’t keep still.
Sir, I’m afraid I’ll forget everything. My hands are shaking.
That’s normal. My heart’s pounding too. But you played the waltz in the dark a week ago. I’m not afraid you’ll forget it.
I can’t wait for it to start. I’m fed up with waiting! The hall is huge, did you see? There are two thousand seats.
Exactly. I’m surprised there are so many people to listen to children.
(coming in) I’m delighted to find you all in one piece! I had to show my badge three times to get in. They took me for a violin thief.
Odile! I’m glad you came all the way here. Is Isabelle in the hall?
In the third row. She’s afraid I’ll faint, so she bought me a bottle of water. As if water cured emotion.
It’s a pity Mrs Roux couldn’t come. She would have been proud of us.
She’s listening on the radio. France Musique is broadcasting the concert live. And I’m sorry she isn’t here, too. But she told me something this morning, on the phone.
She said: “Tell Inès that Lucien is delighted she’s playing his clarinet in Paris. He had never been there.”
(smiles) Then I’m not afraid any more. Well… a little less.
A little fear is good. Henri used to say that a sailor who is never afraid of the sea is a sailor who will drown.
Come on. It’s time. I’m proud of you, whatever happens. On stage!

“Aht”: aspirated “h” (no liaison: “j’ai hâte”, but “la hâte”), long “â”.
After verbs and expressions of EMOTION, the “que” clause takes the SUBJUNCTIVE:
joy: être content / ravi / heureux que
Je suis content que vous soyez venue.
sadness, regret: regretter que, c’est dommage que
C’est dommage que Madame Roux ne puisse pas venir.
fear: avoir peur que, craindre que
Elle a peur que je fasse un malaise.
surprise: être étonné que, s’étonner que
Je suis étonnée qu’il y ait autant de monde.
Nous sommes fiers que vous ayez joué ici.
A typical mistake: the indicative after an emotion, as in English (“I’m glad you are”). In French: “je suis content que tu SOIS”, not “que tu es” ✗.
As with purpose (ch. 61): if the person feeling the emotion is the one doing the action, use “de” + infinitive:
Je suis content que tu sois là.
“Je suis content que je sois là” ✗ — it sounds as odd as “I’m glad that I should be here”.
3. The past infinitive: an emotion about the past
For an action already completed: “de” + avoir / être + participle. With the subjunctive: the past subjunctive (ch. 37).
I’m proud to have played in Paris.
It’s a pity she couldn’t come.
After “avoir peur que” and “craindre que”, careful French adds a “ne” that does NOT negate anything:
I’m afraid it will rain. (NOT “that it won’t rain”!)
I’m afraid it won’t rain. (real negation: ne… pas)
In speech, the expletive “ne” almost always disappears: “J’ai peur qu’il pleuve.” You just need to RECOGNISE it when reading.

On Saturday 5 April, at half past six in the morning, Part-Dieu station had never seen so many children at once. There were sixty of them, with sixty sleeping bags, sixty instrument cases and about a hundred and twenty parents all giving advice at the same time. Julien, list in hand, counted the children once. He found fifty-nine.

He had a second of pure panic. Then he saw Yanis running out of the toilets, his case on his back. He counted again. Sixty. He counted once more, to be safe. Still sixty. Mrs Mansouri, who was watching him, handed him a glass of mint tea. “Drink, Mr Moreau. You’re going to count all the way to Paris, so you need your strength.”

Sami’s father had arrived first, at a quarter to six, with a small sports bag and a thermos. He wore a clean jacket, visibly new. Sami stood next to him, very straight, his flute clutched to his chest. When Julien walked past them, the father put his hand on his heart without saying anything. Julien did the same.

Odile had come in a little blue hat she hadn’t worn for years. She refused to sit on the bench Ioana offered her. “I’m a chaperone,” she declared. “Chaperones stand.” Then, two minutes later, she sat down anyway, explaining it was only to keep an eye on the bags.

Ioana had come with Rose-Hélène to say goodbye. She wasn’t going, for lack of leave, and she regretted it more than she wanted to admit. “I’m glad you’re going,” she told Julien as she kissed him. “And I’m sad not to be going. Both at once.” Rose-Hélène blew into Henri’s harmonica, and the whole platform turned round.

On the TGV, most of the children had never taken such a fast train. Some had never taken a train at all. Yanis counted the tunnels out loud. The girls from the second violins got out a pack of cards. Inès, though, said nothing. She looked out of the window, her clarinet on her knees, as if she were afraid someone would take it from her.

Sami and his father sat side by side, by the window. They watched the fields, the villages, the white Burgundy cows go by, without speaking. From time to time the father pointed at something, and Sami nodded. Julien, walking down the aisle for the sixth time, noticed they were holding hands. He moved on without a word.

In Paris they arrived at the Gare de Lyon, which made the children laugh a lot. “We leave Lyon to arrive at Lyon!” Yanis kept saying. Then came the metro, an experience Julien would never forget: sixty children, sixty cases, two changes of line and a broken escalator. When they finally came out at La Villette, he counted again. Sixty. He nearly cried with relief.

The Philharmonie was a huge silver building, covered in thousands of small bird-shaped plates. The children stopped in the square, mouths open. Radu was waiting for them at the stage door, next to the little van. His eyes were red with tiredness, but he was smiling. “Everything has arrived,” he said. “The cello, the țambal, the double bass. And Rose-Hélène’s flute.”

In the afternoon they had an hour to rehearse in the big hall. It was the first time the children had seen such a place. The balconies rose in waves on all sides, right up to the ceiling, like the walls of an enormous shell. The stage was in the middle, with seats all around, even behind the orchestra. Two thousand empty seats were looking at them.

The children played the Brahms dance timidly, far too softly. They were afraid the sound would get lost in that vastness. Julien stopped the orchestra. Then he did something strange: he asked the children to put down their instruments and lie on the stage, on their backs, to look at the ceiling. Sixty children lay down without understanding.

“You see?” Julien said. “It’s only a ceiling. Higher than ours, but it’s a ceiling. And under this ceiling there’s the same thing as at home: you.” Inès looked for a long time at the big white panels above her. “There’s no window,” she murmured. Yanis, lying next to her, answered without turning his head: “Who cares. She’s in the waltz. You said so yourself.”

When they got up, something had changed. They played the Brahms dance again, and this time the sound filled the hall up to the last balcony. A technician adjusting the lights stopped to listen. At the end he applauded on his own, up there in the dark. The children looked up, surprised, and burst out laughing.

In the evening, at the youth hostel, it was impossible to get them to sleep. There was a pillow fight in the boys’ dormitory, singing in the girls’ dormitory, and an improvised flute concert in the corridor at eleven at night. Mrs Benali confiscated three phones and a torch. At midnight, at last, silence fell.

Radu, for his part, went out onto the pavement to call Lucia. He told her about the metro, the cases, the technician clapping in the dark. Lucia laughed at the other end of the line. “I’m so glad you’re there,” she said. “And so jealous!” Then she added, more quietly: “In a month, it’s us. Are you scared?” Radu looked at the lit windows of the hostel. “No,” he replied. “I can’t wait.”

At three in the morning, Julien, who couldn’t sleep, went out into the corridor. Sami’s father was sitting on a chair in front of his son’s dormitory door, exactly as Odile had suggested. He had his thermos on his knees and he wasn’t sleeping either. He motioned Julien to sit next to him and poured him a coffee.

They talked for a long time, in low voices, with few words. Sami’s father knew about a hundred words of French, and Julien about ten words of Arabic, learned from Mrs Mansouri. But they understood each other. The father took out of his wallet a small, worn photo: the young woman from the living room. “She sang,” he said. “Very well. Sami… like her.”

Then he hummed, very softly, a melody Julien didn’t know. It was a sad, slow song, with notes that rose and fell like waves. Julien listened, holding his breath. When the father fell silent, he took out a pencil and wrote it down from memory, on the back of the list of sixty children.

On Sunday morning, Isabelle came to fetch her mother from the hostel to take her to lunch. She found Odile braiding the hair of three little violinists, sitting on a bunk bed with a comb between her teeth. “Mum, you were supposed to rest.” “I am resting,” Odile replied. “Braiding is like tying sailor’s knots. It’s restful.”

Around noon, in the Parc de la Villette, Julien had another surprise. An old man with white hair was waiting for him on a bench in front of the Philharmonie. It was Olivier Marchand, his former teacher, the one who had offered him a post at the Paris Conservatoire two years earlier. Julien had turned the post down to stay in Lyon. He had been afraid his teacher would hold it against him.

Marchand stood up slowly and hugged him. “I’ve read all the articles,” he said. “The hall, the fake news, the Christmas market. I’m glad you turned down my offer, you know. You’d have been a good teacher in Paris. But in Lyon you’ve become something else. I don’t know what yet. That’s why I came to listen.”

At four o’clock sharp, the lights in the big hall went down. Two thousand people fell silent. The La Duchère orchestra was the third and last of the festival. The first two, from Lille and Marseille, had been warmly applauded. The Lyon children walked on stage in silence, in their black clothes, and sat down without a sound.

In Villeurbanne, at the same moment, Mrs Roux was sitting in her kitchen in front of an old radio, surrounded by four neighbours. She had put on her best dress, as if she were in the hall. On rue d’Austerlitz, Ioana had switched on the living-room radio. Rose-Hélène, on her lap, held Henri’s harmonica. And all over La Duchère, windows had opened and radios had been switched on.

The Brahms dance set off like a galloping horse. The Spanish tune had the two thousand spectators stamping their feet, and a very serious gentleman in the front row even stood up to dance, under the horrified gaze of his wife. Then silence returned. Julien lowered his arms and gave Inès a sign.

She played the first notes of Henri’s waltz alone, in that huge hall, and the sound of Lucien Roux’s clarinet rose to the last balcony. In her Villeurbanne kitchen, Mrs Roux closed her eyes. On rue d’Austerlitz, Rose-Hélène blew into the harmonica at exactly the same moment, the same three notes. Ioana never knew whether it was a coincidence.

To finish, the orchestra played the “Waltz for two women”. At the third verse, as in Lyon, Odile stood up in the front row and whistled the melody with the children. Isabelle tried to hold her back by the sleeve, then gave up and started whistling too. Behind them, other spectators began to hum, without knowing the tune.

When the last note died away, there were three seconds of absolute silence. Then two thousand people rose at once. The applause lasted six minutes. The children no longer knew whether to bow, laugh or cry, so they did all three. Sami, in the back row, raised his flute towards the ceiling, and his father, in the hall, raised his hand towards him.

After the concert, backstage, an elegant woman came up to Julien. She introduced herself: Catherine Dumas, from the Ministry of Culture. “Mr Moreau, I’m delighted to meet you,” she said. “The ministry is preparing a national project inspired by your work. Ten orchestras in ten cities. We’re looking for someone to run it. I’d like you to think about it.”

She handed him a business card. Julien put it in his pocket, next to the list of children and Sami’s father’s song. He didn’t answer. He was afraid of saying yes too quickly, and afraid of saying no too quickly. He only said he first had to bring sixty children back to Lyon, and that this was already a national mission.

On Monday evening, on the platform at Part-Dieu, a crowd was waiting for them. Parents, brothers and sisters, neighbours, Marc Delorme with his notebook, Pierre Duval with a photographer. And, sitting in a wheelchair pushed by her nephew, Mrs Roux, who hadn’t been able to go to Paris but had refused to miss the return.

Inès ran to her before anyone else. She gave her the concert programme, signed by all sixty children. Then she opened her case and showed her the clarinet. “He went to Paris,” she said. “Lucien. He finally went to Paris.” Mrs Roux took the clarinet in her wrinkled hands and kissed it, the way you kiss someone coming back from very far away.

That evening Julien came home exhausted. Ioana was waiting for him in the kitchen. Rose-Hélène had been asleep for a long time, with Henri’s harmonica under her pillow. “Well?” Ioana asked. Julien sat down and emptied his pockets onto the table: the list of children, the song written down at three in the morning, and a business card from the Ministry of Culture.

Ioana read the card twice. Then she put it on the calendar, right next to “15 May. Sea.”, written in pen. “We’ll talk about it at the seaside,” she said. “Not before. First there’s a wedding.” Julien smiled. He was too tired to argue, and anyway he knew she was right. He went to bed, his head full of waltzes and trains.

In the evening, on France Musique, a critic talks about the concert. Listen to the text twice, then read it aloud. At the end you answer 4 questions.
I must admit: I came to the Philharmonie this afternoon without much enthusiasm. A festival of children’s orchestras — I was afraid it would be long, nice, a bit boring. I’m happy to have been wrong.
The strongest moment was the performance by the La Duchère orchestra, from Lyon. Sixty children, many of whom had never left their neighbourhood. I’m surprised this project isn’t talked about more.

They played a Brahms dance with rare energy, then a Spanish tune that had the whole hall stamping. But it was the waltz that changed everything. A little twelve-year-old clarinettist began it alone, and two thousand people held their breath.

Afterwards I was told the story of this waltz, written in 1962 by a young man for his fiancée, and forgotten for sixty years in an old piano. I regret not knowing it before the concert. I would have cried even more.

At the end, an old lady stood up in the front row and began to whistle the melody with the orchestra. The conductor didn’t stop her. On the contrary, he turned towards her and smiled. I still can’t believe it.

It is rare for a concert to move me so much. It’s a pity these children can’t play in Paris more often. I can’t wait for them to come back. And I am proud, for once, to have been a music critic that Sunday.
(“ne pas en revenir” = not to be able to believe it)
De quoi le critique avait-il peur avant le concert ?
Que les enfants ne viennent pas
Qu’a fait la vieille dame au premier rang ?
I can’t wait for them to come back.
